notes: Added q.s. (quantity sufficient): it automatically fills the formula up to 100%.
Above about 8-10% the product starts to feel sticky.
Often used as a natural alternative to silicones. Required HLB is an estimate.
Very resistant to oxidation. Published required-HLB values vary (about 5-11): confirm with supplier.
High in unsaturated fatty acids, so it can go rancid. Pair with an antioxidant such as tocopherol.
Forms a gel network with the emulsifier that holds oil droplets in place. C16 gives a softer feel, C18 a firmer body.
Cetearyl alcohol IS a blend of cetyl (C16) and stearyl (C18) alcohols, so it is the same material as the entry above. Use one or the other.
Builds liquid-crystal (lamellar) structures together with fatty alcohols. Often sold pre-blended with cetearyl alcohol. HLB is an estimate.
Anionic (negatively charged): do not combine with cationic ingredients. Very good at stabilising rich, butter-heavy formulas. HLB is an estimate.
Above about 5% it can leave white marks or drag. Natural starch is food for microbes, so the preservative system must be strong.
Added q.s. until the target pH is reached: measure, don't calculate. Mainly needed when acids or carbomer are present.
Prohibited in LEAVE-ON cosmetics under the ASEAN Cosmetic Directive (and the EU). Rinse-off maximum is 0.0015%. Weak against yeast and mould on its own.
Above about 5% it can turn grainy if the batch cools slowly (fat crystallisation). Cool quickly while stirring.

func: Very light, dry-feel emollient; good solvent
notes: Often used to dissolve UV filters. Required HLB unknown: add it from the supplier TDS.
